claim: Toxoplasma gondii is thought to infect over a quarter of the world's population.
source: Toxoplasma gondii is an intracellular protozoan parasite that is thought to infect over a quarter of the world's population (Pappas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pappas et al., 2009

claim: In intermediate hosts, Toxoplasma parasites remain haploid and transition from a replicative, virulent tachyzoite to an encysted, quasi-dormant bradyzoite.
source: In intermediate hosts, including humans and virtually all other non-feline, warm-blooded animals, Toxoplasma parasites remain haploid and transition from a replicative, virulent tachyzoite to an encysted, quasi-dormant bradyzoite.
evidence: Established knowledge about Toxoplasma life cycle

claim: Acute infection with tachyzoites produces few if any symptoms in healthy human children and adults.
source: Although acute infection with tachyzoites produces few if any symptoms in healthy human children and adults, infected individuals, if left untreated, progress to a chronic stage wherein tachyzoites transition to bradyzoites that can persist for life in neurons and muscle cells.
evidence: Established clinical knowledge about Toxoplasma infection

claim: Bradyzoites can persist for life in neurons and muscle cells.
source: Although acute infection with tachyzoites produces few if any symptoms in healthy human children and adults, infected individuals, if left untreated, progress to a chronic stage wherein tachyzoites transition to bradyzoites that can persist for life in neurons and muscle cells.
evidence: Established knowledge about chronic Toxoplasma infection

claim: When infected individuals become immunocompromised, bradyzoites can reactivate to become tachyzoites, causing severe neurological damage and even death.
source: When infected individuals become immunocompromised, such as in chemotherapy, HIV infection, or organ transplantation (Rabaud et al., 1994; Robert-Gangneux et al., 2015), bradyzoites can reactivate to become tachyzoites, causing severe neurological damage and even death.
evidence: Supported by citations to Rabaud et al., 1994 and Robert-Gangneux et al., 2015

claim: A population-wide study has uncovered significant association of Toxoplasma infection with schizophrenia in chronically infected humans.
source: While no causal link has been established, a population-wide study has uncovered significant association of Toxoplasma infection with schizophrenia in chronically infected humans (Sutterland et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sutterland et al., 2015

claim: Chronic infection in mice has been observed to induce behavioral changes such as loss of aversion to cat urine.
source: Chronic infection in mice has been observed to induce behavioral changes such as loss of aversion to cat urine, which is hypothesized to increase the transmission rate of Toxoplasma to its definitive feline host where sexual reproduction occurs (Vyas et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Vyas et al., 2007

claim: There are no therapeutic interventions to prevent or clear cysts in infected individuals.
source: As there are no therapeutic interventions to prevent or clear cysts in infected individuals, understanding how Toxoplasma transitions through its life stages remains of critical importance.
evidence: Statement of current therapeutic limitations

claim: Bulk transcriptomic analyses of Toxoplasma gondii at distinct asexual stages reveal genetic modules that are expressed in each stage.
source: Bulk transcriptomic analyses of Toxoplasma gondii at distinct asexual stages reveal genetic modules that are expressed in each stage (Buchholz et al., 2011; Manger et al., 1998a; Pittman et al., 2014; Yip, 2007; Cleary et al., 2002; Radke et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2018; Fouts and Boothroyd, 2007)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to previous bulk transcriptomic studies

claim: AP2 transcription factors are thought to play a role in differentiation.
source: Bulk transcriptomic analyses of Toxoplasma gondii at distinct asexual stages reveal genetic modules that are expressed in each stage (Buchholz et al., 2011; Manger et al., 1998a; Pittman et al., 2014; Yip, 2007; Cleary et al., 2002; Radke et al., 2005; Chen et al., 2018; Fouts and Boothroyd, 2007), including AP2 transcription factors that are thought to play a role in differentiation (Hong et al., 2017; White et al., 2014)
evidence: Supported by citations to Hong et al., 2017 and White et al., 2014

claim: Transitioning parasites convert to the bradyzoite stage asynchronously and display a high degree of heterogeneity along the developmental pathway and in gene expression.
source: however, transitioning parasites convert to the bradyzoite stage asynchronously and display a high degree of heterogeneity along the developmental pathway and in gene expression (Soete et al., 1993; Watts et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Soete et al., 1993 and Watts et al., 2015

claim: Parasites within the same tissue cysts have been shown to display heterogeneity in the expression of bradyzoite marker proteins.
source: Furthermore, parasites within the same tissue cysts have been shown to display heterogeneity in the expression of bradyzoite marker proteins (Ferguson et al., 1994).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferguson et al., 1994

claim: The transition of tachyzoites to the bradyzoite stage results in an overwhelming majority of mature bradyzoites in the G1 phase of the cell cycle that divide slowly, if at all.
source: The transition of tachyzoites to the bradyzoite stage results in an overwhelming majority of mature bradyzoites in the G1 phase of the cell cycle that divide slowly, if at all (Radke et al., 2003; Sinai et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Radke et al., 2003 and Sinai et al., 2016

claim: Tachyzoites exhibit slower growth kinetics immediately prior to the bradyzoite transition.
source: Furthermore, tachyzoites exhibit slower growth kinetics immediately prior to the bradyzoite transition (Radke et al., 2003; Jerome et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citations to Radke et al., 2003 and Jerome et al., 1998

claim: Parasites exit the cell cycle to differentiate into bradyzoites, a pattern consistent with developmental processes in several other eukaryotic organisms.
source: This suggests that parasites exit the cell cycle to differentiate into bradyzoites, a pattern consistent with developmental processes in several other eukaryotic organisms (Ali et al., 2011; Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ali et al., 2011 and Kim et al., 2010

claim: Droplet and FACS-based approaches have already been applied towards multicellular parasites such as Schistosoma to reveal developmental changes within different hosts.
source: Droplet and FACS-based approaches have already been applied towards multicellular parasites such as Schistosoma to reveal developmental changes within different hosts (Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018

claim: scRNA-seq has revealed a surprising degree of heterogeneity in Plasmodium.
source: Recently, scRNA-seq has revealed a surprising degree of heterogeneity in another apicomplexan parasite, Plasmodium (Reid et al., 2018; Ngara et al., 2018; Poran et al., 2017; Howick et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Reid et al., 2018; Ngara et al., 2018; Poran et al., 2017; Howick et al., 2019

claim: Analyses derived from single-parasite measurements uncovered rare and critical transition events in parasite development that were undetectable in bulk measurements.
source: Analyses derived from these single-parasite measurements uncovered rare and critical transition events in parasite development that were undetectable in bulk measurements.
evidence: Inference based on cited scRNA-seq studies of Plasmodium

claim: The study performed scRNA-seq on >5,400 Toxoplasma in both tachyzoite and bradyzoite stages using three widely studied strains.
source: Here, we applied single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) on >5,400 Toxoplasma in both tachyzoite and bradyzoite stages using three widely studied strains to construct a comprehensive atlas of cell-cycle and asexual development, revealing hidden states and transcriptional factors associated with each developmental stage.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental approach in abstract

claim: Analysis of SAG1-related sequence (SRS) antigenic repertoire reveals a highly heterogeneous, sporadic expression pattern unexplained by measurement noise, cell cycle, or asexual development.
source: Analysis of SAG1-related sequence (SRS) antigenic repertoire reveals a highly heterogeneous, sporadic expression pattern unexplained by measurement noise, cell cycle, or asexual development.
evidence: Direct statement of finding in abstract

claim: AP2IX-1 was identified as a transcription factor that controls the switching from the ubiquitous SAG1 to rare surface antigens not previously observed in tachyzoites.
source: Furthermore, we identified AP2IX-1 as a transcription factor that controls the switching from the ubiquitous SAG1 to rare surface antigens not previously observed in tachyzoites.
evidence: Direct statement of finding in abstract

claim: Comparative analysis between Toxoplasma and Plasmodium scRNA-seq results reveals concerted expression of gene sets, despite fundamental differences in cell division.
source: In addition, comparative analysis between Toxoplasma and Plasmodium scRNA-seq results reveals concerted expression of gene sets, despite fundamental differences in cell division.
evidence: Direct statement of finding in abstract

claim: Smart-seq2 generally has higher sensitivity than competing droplet-based approaches.
source: Based on benchmark comparisons, Smart-seq2 generally has higher sensitivity than competing droplet-based approaches (Svensson et al., 2017; Ziegenhain et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Svensson et al., 2017 and Ziegenhain et al., 2017

claim: Single Toxoplasma gondii parasites are at least 50-fold smaller in volume than a typical mammalian cell.
source: We reasoned that sensitive measurement is crucial in our study, given that single Toxoplasma gondii parasites are at least 50-fold smaller in volume than a typical mammalian cell, and thus the average parasite gene is likely expressed with much lower copy number per cell than a typical mammalian gene.
evidence: Statement of biological fact used to justify methodological choice

claim: The reagent cost in 384-well plates was reduced effectively by ten-fold compared to the 96-well format.
source: We reduced the reagent cost in 384-well plates effectively by ten-fold compared to the 96-well format.
evidence: Direct statement of methodological achievement

claim: The rate of doublet events is below 1%.
source: Across all 301 wells that we measured, we observed the presence of both GFP and mCherry mRNA in only one well, indicating that the rate of doublet events is below 1% (Figure 1—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1a

claim: The detected amount of SAG1 mRNA present in wells containing single, eight, or fifty RH fell into the expected distributions based on the number of parasites sorted, without signs of saturation.
source: The detected amount of SAG1 mRNA present in wells containing single, eight, or fifty RH fell into the expected distributions based on the number of parasites sorted, without signs of saturation, indicating that the assay is capable of quantitative measurement at the single Toxoplasma level.
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1b

claim: 729 RH strain single Toxoplasma parasites from asynchronous populations were sequenced, with 612 passing quality control.
source: We then proceeded to sort parasites into 384-well based on live/dead staining and sequence 729 RH (612 passed quality control) strain single Toxoplasma parasites from asynchronous populations grown under tachyzoite conditions.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data

claim: 287 RH parasites were sorted and sequenced into 96-well plate, with 237 passing quality control.
source: We also sorted and sequenced 287 RH parasites (237 passed quality control) into 96-well plate for comparison, which we will discuss further in another section.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data

claim: 2655 Pru single parasites were collected, with 2198 passing quality control.
source: For Pru and ME49 strains, we collected parasites at several time points post alkaline treatment which induces differentiation from tachyzoites to bradyzoites to follow changes in their expression profiles during in vitro development (Materials and methods), yielding 2655 Pru (2198 passed quality control) and 1828 ME49 (1552 passed quality control) single parasites.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data

claim: 1828 ME49 single parasites were collected, with 1552 passing quality control.
source: For Pru and ME49 strains, we collected parasites at several time points post alkaline treatment which induces differentiation from tachyzoites to bradyzoites to follow changes in their expression profiles during in vitro development (Materials and methods), yielding 2655 Pru (2198 passed quality control) and 1828 ME49 (1552 passed quality control) single parasites.
evidence: Direct statement of experimental data

claim: Many genes encoding Toxoplasma secretion factors and surface proteins are evolutionary products of gene duplication events.
source: Because many genes encoding Toxoplasma secretion factors and surface proteins are evolutionary products of gene duplication events (Reid, 2015), we expected high sequence similarity amongst a substantial portion of the parasite genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Reid, 2015

claim: On average, each sequenced parasite contains 30–50% reads that mapped to Toxoplasma genes encoding proteins.
source: On average, each sequenced parasite contains 30–50% reads that mapped to Toxoplasma genes encoding proteins (top panel in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b

claim: Most of the unmapped reads are from Toxoplasma's 28 s ribosomal RNA.
source: Most of the unmapped reads are from Toxoplasma's 28 s ribosomal RNA.
evidence: Direct statement based on data analysis

claim: The relatively high rate of rRNA contamination was also observed in single-parasite RNA sequencing of Plasmodium.
source: The relatively high rate of rRNA contamination was also observed in single-parasite RNA sequencing of Plasmodium (Reid et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reid et al., 2018

claim: On average 862, 1290, and 970 genes per parasite with greater than or equal to two read counts were detected in the RH, Pru, and ME49 datasets, respectively.
source: After filtering ERCC spike-in and rRNA genes, we detected on average 862, 1290, and 970 genes per parasite with greater than or equal to two read counts (Materials and methods) in the RH, Pru, and ME49 datasets, respectively (bottom panel in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2b

claim: Characterization of measurement sensitivity based on logistic regression modeling of ERCC spike-in standards reveals a 50% detection rate of 17, 17, and 26 molecules for RH, Pru, and ME49 datasets, respectively.
source: Characterization of our measurement sensitivity based on logistic regression modeling of ERCC spike-in standards (Materials and methods) (Lönnberg et al., 2017) reveals a 50% detection rate of 17, 17, and 26 molecules for RH, Pru, and ME49 datasets, respectively (top panels in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c and citation to Lönnberg et al., 2017

claim: The sensitivity of the 384-well Smart-seq2 measurement is comparable to the previously reported range for the 96-well format.
source: The sensitivity of our 384-well Smart-seq2 measurement is comparable to the previously reported range for the 96-well format (Ziegenhain et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ziegenhain et al., 2017

claim: The linear dynamic range of scRNA-seq measurement spans over three orders of magnitude.
source: We determined that the linear dynamic range of our scRNA-seq measurement spans over three orders of magnitude (bottom panels in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2c

claim: The first two principal components reveal a circular trajectory that coincides with relative DNA content.
source: Interestingly, the first two principal components (PCs) reveal a circular trajectory that coincides with relative DNA content, determined using a cell permeable DNA content stain (top panel in Figure 2a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a

claim: Unsupervised neighborhood clustering identified five distinct clusters of parasites based on their transcriptional profiles.
source: Unsupervised neighborhood clustering identified five distinct clusters of parasites based on their transcriptional profiles (middle panel in Figure 2a) (Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a

claim: RNA velocity vector field indicates a net 'counter-clockwise' flow of transcriptional changes.
source: We computed RNA velocity to infer transcriptional dynamics (La Manno et al., 2018; Wolf et al., 2018) and the velocity vector field indicates a net 'counter-clockwise' flow of transcriptional changes (bottom panel in Figure 2a) (Materials and methods).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2a and citations to La Manno et al., 2018 and Wolf et al., 2018

claim: Unsupervised clustering identified two distinct clusters in G1 state, designated as G1a and G1b.
source: Unsupervised clustering identified two distinct clusters in G1 state, which we have designated as G1a and G1b.
evidence: Direct statement of clustering results

claim: The G1a cluster is highly enriched for the expression of metabolic genes such as phenylalanine hydroxylase (TGGT1_411100) and pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase (TGGT1_236070), as well as invasion-related secreted factors such as MIC2 (TGGT1_201780), MIC3 (TGGT1_319560), and MIC11 (TGGT1_204530).
source: The G1a cluster is highly enriched for the expression of metabolic genes such as phenylalanine hydroxylase (TGGT1_411100) and pyrroline-5-carboxylate reductase (TGGT1_236070), as well as invasion-related secreted factors such as MIC2 (TGGT1_201780), MIC3 (TGGT1_319560), and MIC11 (TGGT1_204530).
evidence: Direct statement of differential expression analysis results

claim: G1b cluster is enriched for the expression of 3-ketoacyl reductase (TGGT1_217740) and cytidine and deoxycytidylate deaminase (TGGT1_200430), as well as numerous uncharacterized proteins.
source: On the other hand, G1b cluster is enriched for the expression of 3-ketoacyl reductase (TGGT1_217740) and cytidine and deoxycytidylate deaminase (TGGT1_200430), as well as numerous uncharacterized proteins (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Direct statement of differential expression analysis results

claim: The relative abundance of G1a, G1b, S, M, and C states were determined to be 18%, 32%, 28%, 15%, and 7%, respectively.
source: The relative abundance of G1a, G1b, S, M, and C states were determined to be 18%, 32%, 28%, 15%, and 7%, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative analysis results

claim: The correlation between the scRNA-seq data of asynchronous parasites and previously published bulk transcriptomic measurement suggests strong agreement in cluster assignment and cell cycle state identification.
source: Without chemical synchronization, the correlation between the scRNA-seq data of asynchronous parasites and previously published bulk transcriptomic measurement suggests strong agreement in cluster assignment and cell cycle state identification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1b

claim: 63.5% of genes annotated as rhoptry (ROP) or rhoptry neck (RON) are assigned pseudotime cluster 3, while the remaining 36.5% rhoptry genes are assigned pseudotime clusters 1 or 2.
source: For example, 63.5% of genes annotated as rhoptry (ROP) or rhoptry neck (RON) are assigned pseudotime cluster 3, while the remaining 36.5% rhoptry genes are assigned pseudotime clusters 1 or 2 (Figure 2—figure supplement 1e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1e

claim: Genes annotated as ROP33 and ROP34 are assigned to cluster 2 instead of cluster 3.
source: Specifically, genes annotated as ROP33 and ROP34, based on their homology to genes encoding known rhoptry proteins, are assigned to cluster 2 instead of cluster 3 (left panel in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: ROP33 and ROP34 have been experimentally determined to be non-rhoptry-localizing proteins.
source: Recent reports have experimentally determined these two to be non-rhoptry-localizing proteins. This is consistent with our observation of discordance between their and known ROPs' expression profiles along the pseudotime (Beraki et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Beraki et al., 2019

claim: TGGT1_218270 and TGGT1_230350 have been shown to encode bona fide rhoptry and rhoptry neck proteins, now designated as ROP48 and RON11, respectively.
source: Through analysis of pseudotime clustering, we also identified genes not annotated as ROPs within the ROP-dominated cluster 3, such as TGGT1_218270 and TGGT1_230350, that have recently been shown to encode bona fide rhoptry and rhoptry neck proteins, now designated as ROP48 and RON11, respectively (Camejo et al., 2014; Beck et al., 2013) (left panel in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by citations to Camejo et al., 2014 and Beck et al., 2013

claim: IMC2a peaks in expression level in G1, while the majority of inner-membrane complex (IMC) genes are expressed towards the M/C phase of the cell cycle.
source: As another example, IMC2a peaks in expression level in G1, while the majority of inner-membrane complex (IMC) genes are expressed towards the M/C phase of the cell cycle (right panel in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1f

claim: A recent report has proposed reannotation of IMC2a as a dense granule (GRA) protein (GRA44) based on subcellular localization.
source: A recent report has proposed reannotation of IMC2a as a dense granule (GRA) protein (GRA44) based on subcellular localization (Coffey et al., 2018), which is consistent with our unsupervised group assignment of IMC2a as falling in cluster one where GRA genes dominate.
evidence: Supported by citation to Coffey et al., 2018

claim: Projection of the first two PCs of uninduced Pru tachyzoites (Day 0) reveals the expected circular projection.
source: Projection of the first two PCs of uninduced Pru tachyzoites (Day 0) reveals the expected circular projection (Figure 3—figure supplement 1a), presumably reflecting cell cycle progression as seen for the RH tachyzoites, described above.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1a

claim: The uninduced population of Pru is composed of 28%, 41%, 21%, 7%, and 3% parasites in G1a, G1b, S, M, and C states, respectively.
source: Comparable to what we observed in RH, cell cycle prediction reveals that the uninduced population of Pru is composed of 28%, 41%, 21%, 7%, and 3% parasites in G1a, G1b, S, M, and C states, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement of quantitative analysis results

claim: Most induced Pru parasites (Day 3–7) are in the G1 state with a predominance of G1b.
source: Consistent with previous observation (Jerome et al., 1998), our data show most induced Pru parasites (Day 3–7) are in the G1 state with a predominance of G1b (Figure 3—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1b and citation to Jerome et al., 1998

claim: Unsupervised clustering revealed six distinct clusters of parasites, labeled P1-6.
source: Unsupervised clustering revealed six distinct clusters of parasites, which we label P1-6 (Figure 3a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3a

claim: Cluster formations partially correlate with treatment time points and cell cycle states.
source: Cluster formations partially correlate with treatment time points and cell cycle states (Figure 3b; Figure 3—figure supplement 1c), suggesting that the asexual differentiation program overlaps with cell cycle regulation in Toxoplasma, as proposed previously (Radke et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3b and Figure 3—figure supplement 1c, and citation to Radke et al., 2003

claim: Elevated expression of previously described 'early' bradyzoite marker genes in induced parasites was observed, including SRS44 (CST1) and BAG1, with a concomitant reduction in expression of SRS29B (SAG1).
source: We stratified the datasets by days post alkaline induction (dpi) and observed elevated expression of previously described 'early' bradyzoite marker genes in induced parasites, including SRS44 (CST1) and BAG1, with a concomitant reduction in expression of SRS29B (SAG1), a tachyzoite-specific surface marker gene (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2

claim: The abundance of SAG1+ parasites (72%) in the induced population suggests that either the depletion of SAG1 mRNA is relatively slow or the asexual transition induced by alkaline treatment is highly asynchronous.
source: The abundance of SAG1+ parasites (72%) in the induced population suggests two possible interpretations: (1) the depletion of SAG1 mRNA is relatively slow and we are measuring SAG1 transcripts made when the parasites were still tachyzoites, or (2) the asexual transition induced by alkaline treatment is highly asynchronous.
evidence: Inference based on quantitative data analysis

claim: RNA velocity analysis suggests that P3 may be a fate decision point as the trajectory trifurcates into either P4 (cell cycle), P1, or P2.
source: Interestingly, RNA velocity analysis suggests that P3 may be a fate decision point as the trajectory trifurcates into either P4 (cell cycle), P1, or P2 as evident by the net transcriptional flow (compare Figure 3a to right panel in Figure 3b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3a and Figure 3b

claim: P1 cluster cells are enriched for expression of bradyzoite-specific genes while P2-5 are enriched for that of tachyzoite-specific or cell cycle-associated genes.
source: P1 cluster cells are enriched for expression of bradyzoite-specific genes while P2-5 are enriched for that of tachyzoite-specific or cell cycle-associated genes (Figure 3c–d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3c-d

claim: A small portion of BAG1+ bradyzoites (7.1%) are annotated as either S, M, or C states, indicating that they are replicating.
source: In our scRNA-seq data, we also observe a small portion of BAG1+ bradyzoites (7.1%) annotated as either S, M, or C states, indicating that they are replicating (Figure 3—figure supplement 1d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1d

claim: The data supports the notion that bradyzoites can undergo cell cycle progression.
source: Our data supports the notion that bradyzoites can undergo cell cycle progression (Watts et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by data and citation to Watts et al., 2015

claim: AP2Ib-1, AP2IX-1, AP2IX-6, and AP2VI-2 are over-expressed in P1, suggesting their potential roles in the regulation of developmental transition.
source: In particular, we identify AP2Ib-1, AP2IX-1, AP2IX-6, and AP2VI-2 as over-expressed in P1, suggesting their potential roles in the regulation of developmental transition, while AP2IX-9, AP2X-8, AP2VIIa-6, AP2XI-1, AP2IX-3, AP2VIII-7, and AP2-domain protein TGME49_215895 (not yet assigned a formal AP2 number), are highly expressed in P6, hinting at their possible roles in defining this distinct cluster of parasites.
evidence: Inference based on differential expression data shown in Figure 3e

claim: AP2IX-9, AP2X-8, AP2VIIa-6, AP2XI-1, AP2IX-3, AP2VIII-7, and AP2-domain protein TGME49_215895 are highly expressed in P6, hinting at their possible roles in defining this distinct cluster of parasites.
source: In particular, we identify AP2Ib-1, AP2IX-1, AP2IX-6, and AP2VI-2 as over-expressed in P1, suggesting their potential roles in the regulation of developmental transition, while AP2IX-9, AP2X-8, AP2VIIa-6, AP2XI-1, AP2IX-3, AP2VIII-7, and AP2-domain protein TGME49_215895 (not yet assigned a formal AP2 number), are highly expressed in P6, hinting at their possible roles in defining this distinct cluster of parasites.
evidence: Inference based on differential expression data shown in Figure 3e

claim: The most highly expressed genes in P6 include genes enriched in P2 as well as bradyzoite-specific genes found in P1.
source: The most highly expressed genes in P6 include genes enriched in P2 as well as bradyzoite-specific genes found in P1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3c

claim: Comparison of scRNA-seq data to previous bulk transcriptomic measurement in tachyzoites, tissue cyst, or isolates at the beginning or the end of sexual cycle showed no specific enrichment in known developmental stages for P6.
source: Comparison of our data to previous bulk transcriptomic measurement in tachyzoites, tissue cyst, or isolates at the beginning or the end of sexual cycle showed no specific enrichment in known developmental stages (Figure 3—figure supplement 3b; Ramakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3b and citation to Ramakrishnan et al., 2019

claim: Based on their expression, P6 forms a distinct sub-population of parasites which suggests that alkaline induced Toxoplasma may be more heterogeneous than previously thought.
source: Instead, we show that based on their expression, P6 forms a distinct sub-population of parasites which suggests that alkaline induced Toxoplasma may be more heterogeneous than previously thought.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: Unsupervised clustering revealed five distinct clusters in ME49 which share significant overlap in expression patterns with Pru.
source: Unsupervised clustering revealed five distinct clusters in ME49 which share significant overlap in expression patterns with Pru (Figure 3—figure supplement 4a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4a

claim: Matrix correlation of batch-corrected expression across the two strains demonstrate analogous mapping for most, but not all cluster identities.
source: Matrix correlation of batch-corrected expression across the two strains demonstrate analogous mapping for most, but not all cluster identities (Figure 3—figure supplement 4b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4b

claim: P6-specific genes are not enriched in any cluster in ME49, suggesting that P6 state is not conserved across the two type II strains.
source: Curiously, P6-specific genes (green panels in Figure 3—figure supplement 4c) are not enriched in any cluster in ME49, suggesting that P6 state is not conserved across the two type II strains.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4c

claim: The Toxoplasma gondii genome encodes a family of over 120 SAG1-related sequence (SRS) proteins that fall into distinct subfamilies.
source: The Toxoplasma gondii genome encodes a family of over 120 SAG1-related sequence (SRS) proteins that fall into distinct subfamilies; most or all of these are presumed to be surface antigens based on their sequence similarities, including the presence of a predicted GPI-addition signal (Manger et al., 1998b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manger et al., 1998b

claim: Most or all SRS proteins are presumed to be surface antigens based on their sequence similarities, including the presence of a predicted GPI-addition signal.
source: The Toxoplasma gondii genome encodes a family of over 120 SAG1-related sequence (SRS) proteins that fall into distinct subfamilies; most or all of these are presumed to be surface antigens based on their sequence similarities, including the presence of a predicted GPI-addition signal (Manger et al., 1998b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Manger et al., 1998b

claim: Existing data on developmentally regulated expression of SRSs including SAG1 (SRS29B) and SRS16B lend support to the hypothesis that SRSs constitute an antigenic repertoire that contribute to evasion of host adaptive immunity response.
source: Whether SRSs constitute an antigenic repertoire that contribute to evasion of host adaptive immunity response is unclear; however, existing data on developmentally regulated expression of SRSs including SAG1 (SRS29B) and SRS16B lend support to that hypothesis (Kim and Boothroyd, 2005; Kim et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kim and Boothroyd, 2005 and Kim et al., 2007

claim: Most SRS genes were detected in only a few sporadic cells in 384-well plates.
source: In the experiments using 384-well plates, we noted that most SRS genes were detected in only a few sporadic cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1a)
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1a

claim: 96-well Smart-seq2 achieved ~40% sensitivity of detection for single molecules of ERCC spike-ins, compared to 14% sensitivity obtained in the 384-well experiments.
source: To increase our sensitivity, therefore, we performed scRNA-seq of extracellular Toxoplasma in 96-well plates which achieved ~40% sensitivity of detection for single molecules of ERCC spike-ins, compared to 14% sensitivity that we obtained in the 384-well experiments, at roughly equivalent sequencing depth (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4a

claim: On average 984 genes with read counts equal to or greater than two were measured in 96-well plates, up from 862 genes in 384-well plates.
source: We also measured on average 984 genes with read counts equal to or greater than two in 96-well plates, up from 862 genes in 384-well plates (Figure 4—figure supplement 1c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1c

claim: Analysis of the 96-well plates data show that the vast majority of SRS genes are detected in only a small fraction of the population.
source: Analysis of the resulting 96-well plates data show that the vast majority of SRS genes are detected in only a small fraction of the population (Figure 4b), similar to what we observed in 384-well experiments.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4b

claim: SRSs are detected at a substantially lower rate when compared to ERCC spike-ins, indicating that the variation of SRS detection cannot be explained by measurement noise.
source: The results show that SRSs are indeed detected at a substantially lower rate when compared to ERCC spike-ins (Figure 4c), indicating that the variation of SRS detection cannot be explained by measurement noise.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4c

claim: Compared to most other genes, SRSs are expressed in a significantly smaller fraction of the population and at a relatively lower abundance.
source: Compared to most other genes, SRSs are expressed in a significantly smaller fraction of the population and at a relatively lower abundance (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d-e).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1d-e

claim: Apart from a few known SRSs, most SRSs do not co-vary with cell cycle or asexual development.
source: We show that apart from a few known SRSs, most SRSs do not co-vary with cell cycle or asexual development, which suggests that the sporadic nature of SRS expression may hint at a different biological role for their variation, beyond cell cycle and asexual development, as discussed further below (Figure 4d).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 4d

claim: A lone cell in the 384-well dataset of RH had no detectable level of SRS29B (SAG1), which was otherwise ubiquitously and abundantly expressed in all tachyzoites.
source: In examining our data, we were struck by a lone cell in the 384-well dataset of RH that had no detectable level of SRS29B (SAG1), which was otherwise ubiquitously and abundantly expressed in all tachyzoites (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5a

claim: The SAG1- cell's gene count and read depth were similar to its cohort.
source: We wondered if this cell was damaged or unhealthy but its gene count and read depth were similar to its cohort (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5b

claim: The SAG1- cell lacks expression of the most abundant tachyzoite-specific and bradyzoite-specific genes; instead, its gene expression most closely resembles the sexual stages from cat intestinal isolates, including abundant expression of a cat-stage SRS, SRS22C.
source: Further analysis of this SAG1- cell's transcriptome revealed that it lacks expression of the most abundant tachyzoite-specific and bradyzoite-specific genes; instead, its gene expression most closely resembles the sexual stages from cat intestinal isolates, including abundant expression of a cat-stage SRS, SRS22C (Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Within the set of genes uniquely expressed in the SAG1- cell are AP2IX-1 and AP2III-4 which suggest a possible role for one or both of these transcription factors in regulating the transcript differences observed in this outlier.
source: Within the set of genes uniquely expressed in the SAG1- cell are AP2IX-1 and AP2III-4 which suggest a possible role for one or both of these transcription factors in regulating the transcript differences observed in this outlier.
evidence: Inference based on data shown in Figure 5c

claim: Immunofluorescence assay revealed a reduction of SAG1 surface protein expression within ~18–20 hr after transfection with AP2IX-1.
source: To test this hypothesis, we transiently expressed AP2IX-1 under the control of a strong promoter in RH parasites (Figure 5d). Consistent with our hypothesis, immunofluorescence assay (IFA) revealed a reduction of SAG1 surface protein expression within ~18–20 hr after transfection (Figure 5e–f)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5d-f

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR showed significantly higher mRNA expression for several of the genes that were upregulated in the SAG1- cell: namely, 207965, 222305, 205210, and SRS22C, the latter being over 1000-fold higher in the transfected population than control.
source: while quantitative RT-PCR showed significantly higher mRNA expression for several of the genes that were upregulated in the SAG1- cell: namely, 207965, 222305, 205210, and SRS22C, the latter being over 1000-fold higher in the transfected population than control (Figure 5g).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5g

claim: AP2IX-1 induction can control the switching of surface antigens.
source: As SRS22C is predicted to be a surface antigen like the rest of SRS (Gajria et al., 2008), this suggests that AP2IX-1 induction can control the switching of surface antigens.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data and citation to Gajria et al., 2008

claim: 1830 one-to-one orthologous genes were identified between Plasmodium berghei and Toxoplasma gondii Pru.
source: Toward this end, we first identified 1830 one-to-one orthologous genes between Plasmodium berghei and Toxoplasma gondii Pru (Figure 6—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1a

claim: The vast majority of orthologous genes are not surface adhesion factors or effector molecules in Toxoplasma.
source: As expected, the vast majority of orthologous genes are not surface adhesion factors or effector molecules in Toxoplasma (Figure 6—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1b

claim: In the integrated projection space, mutually similar clusters of cells in the two datasets are brought close together, while organism-specific cell types are not.
source: In this integrated projection space, mutually similar clusters of cells in the two datasets are brought close together, while organism-specific cell types are not (Figure 6a).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6a

claim: Transitional dynamics of the parasitic development are preserved in the integrated projection.
source: Transitional dynamics of the parasitic development are preserved in the integrated projection, as separation of the original cluster assignment indicates (Figure 6b).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 6b

claim: The pre-erythrocytic stages of Plasmodium (sporozoite and merozoites) most closely match the 'G1 a' stage of Toxoplasma.
source: For example, the pre-erythrocytic stages of Plasmodium (sporozoite and merozoites) most closely match the 'G1 a' stage of Toxoplasma.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis shown in Figure 6c-d

claim: Both Plasmodium pre-erythrocytic stages and Toxoplasma G1a stage are not actively replicating DNA and express high levels of ribosomal and mitochondrial genes.
source: Both parasites at these stages are not actively replicating DNA and express high levels of ribosomal and mitochondrial genes.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis

claim: The ring stage of Plasmodium most closely matches the 'G1 b' phase of Toxoplasma because they both express high levels of ribosomal genes with minimal expression of IMC-related and microtubule-related genes.
source: Meanwhile, the ring stage of Plasmodium most closely matches the 'G1 b' phase of Toxoplasma because they both express high levels of ribosomal genes with minimal expression of IMC-related and microtubule-related genes.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis

claim: Exo-erythrocytic form (EEF), microgametes (male), and trophozoite stages of Plasmodium berghei most closely match the 'S' phase of Toxoplasma cell cycle because they express DNA-replication factors and centrosome components.
source: Exo-erythrocytic form (EEF), microgametes (male), and trophozoite stages of Plasmodium berghei most closely match the 'S' phase of Toxoplasma cell cycle. This is because they express DNA-replication factors and centrosome components, which are required for condensation and segregation of chromosomes.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis

claim: The schizont stage of Plasmodium most closely resembles the 'M' and 'C' phases due to the expression of microtubule, centrosome, and IMC genes.
source: Intriguingly, the schizont stage of Plasmodium most closely resembles the 'M' and 'C' phases due to the expression of microtubule, centrosome, and IMC genes.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis

claim: While the cellular morphology and replication strategies may differ drastically between Plasmodium and Toxoplasma, the cellular state, as defined by the transcriptomic profiles, can bear striking analogy and resemblance in the course of asexual replication.
source: Our results indicate that while the cellular morphology and replication strategies may differ drastically between the two parasites, the cellular state, as defined by the transcriptomic profiles, can bear striking analogy and resemblance in the course of asexual replication.
evidence: Inference based on comparative analysis

claim: An interactive single-cell atlas for Toxoplasma gondii was constructed at http://st-atlas.org.
source: Toward enabling the larger scientific community to take advantage of the scRNA-seq data we collected on the three Toxoplasma strains, we have constructed an interactive single-cell atlas for Toxoplasma gondii (http://st-atlas.org) using Bokeh and Javascript.
evidence: Direct statement of resource creation

claim: Two distinct 1N transcriptional states were found in cycling parasites which are called G1a and G1b, concurring with what was previously reported in bulk analyses of Toxoplasma.
source: We found the existence of two distinct 1N transcriptional states in cycling parasites which we call G1a and G1b, concurring with what was previously reported in bulk analyses of Toxoplasma (Behnke et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by data and citation to Behnke et al., 2010

claim: Bradyzoites are found predominantly in G1b but not in G1a, suggesting the possibility of a putative checkpoint between these two phases that may also play a role in regulating the developmental transition.
source: Interestingly, bradyzoites are found predominantly in G1b but not in G1a, suggesting the possibility of a putative checkpoint between these two phases that may also play a role in regulating the developmental transition.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: A cluster of cells, labeled P6, was discovered in the differentiating Pru parasites that is distinct from the rest of the alkaline-induced population of cells.
source: We discovered a cluster of cells, labeled P6, in the differentiating Pru parasites that is distinct from the rest of the alkaline-induced population of cells.
evidence: Direct statement of finding

claim: P6 cluster constitutes 21% of the alkaline-induced population.
source: Constituting 21% of the alkaline-induced population, the P6 cluster is marked by a set of genes that were previously detected by bulk transcriptomics in bradyzoites of tissue cysts (Ramakrishnan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by data and citation to Ramakrishnan et al., 2019

claim: The P6 expression profile is intermediate to P2 tachyzoites and P1 bradyzoite clusters.
source: We found that the P6 expression profile is intermediate to P2 tachyzoites and P1 bradyzoite clusters.
evidence: Direct statement based on data analysis

claim: The genes enriched in P6 overlap with a subset of canonical bradyzoite marker genes including LDH2 and SRS35A, albeit expressed at a lower level than in P1.
source: Interestingly, the genes enriched in P6 overlap with a subset of canonical bradyzoite marker genes including LDH2 and SRS35A, albeit expressed at a lower level than in P1 (Figure 3c).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3c

claim: A gradual increase in the proportion of P6 cells was observed as induction proceeded from day 3 to day 7.
source: In addition, we observed a gradual increase in the proportion of P6 cells as induction proceeded from day 3 to day 7.
evidence: Direct statement based on data analysis

claim: One possible explanation for the emergence of P6 cluster is a reverted conversion from bradyzoites to tachyzoites in which alkaline stress fails to maintain the bradyzoite state.
source: Taken together, one possible explanation for the emergence of P6 cluster is a reverted conversion from bradyzoites to tachyzoites in which alkaline stress fails to maintain the bradyzoite state. Our data and previous reports are consistent with this interpretation (Weiss et al., 1998).
evidence: Speculation supported by data and citation to Weiss et al., 1998

claim: RNA velocity analysis in the Pru data does not reveal a strong transcriptional flow between P1 and P6.
source: RNA velocity analysis in the Pru data does not reveal a strong transcriptional flow between P1 and P6.
evidence: Direct statement based on data analysis

claim: P6 appears to transcriptionally transition from P2 tachyzoites.
source: Rather, P6 appears to transcriptionally transition from P2 tachyzoites.
evidence: Inference based on RNA velocity analysis

claim: The P1 bradyzoites and P6 parasites are either distinct and separate developmental trajectories, or the transition from P1 to P6 is a rapid and rare event.
source: Thus, the P1 bradyzoites and P6 parasites are either distinct and separate developmental trajectories, or the transition from P1 to P6 is a rapid and rare event.
evidence: Inference based on data analysis

claim: 96-well Smart-seq2 greatly improved measurement sensitivity over the 384-well format, likely due to changes in the input mRNA concentration.
source: To quantify the variation of SRSs, which are generally expressed at low copy number, we performed 96-well Smart-seq2, which greatly improved measurement sensitivity over the 384-well format, likely due to changes in the input mRNA concentration.
evidence: Inference based on experimental comparison

claim: scRNA-seq analysis identified an atypical co-expression pattern in an in vitro RH 'tachyzoite' that is indicative of sexual development, which has not been previously observed in these culture conditions.
source: Very surprisingly, our scRNA-seq analysis identified an atypical co-expression pattern in an in vitro RH 'tachyzoite' that is indicative of sexual development, which has not been previously observed in these culture conditions.
evidence: Direct statement of finding

claim: At least the beginnings of sexual developmental can spontaneously occur even in the absence of the cat intestinal environment or other chemical cues.
source: This suggests that at least the beginnings of sexual developmental can spontaneously occur even in the absence of the cat intestinal environment or other chemical cues.
evidence: Inference based on single-cell data

claim: AP2IX-1 is sufficient to drive a switching of surface antigen expression toward that resembling the sexual stages of the parasite.
source: Combined with transient expression experiments, the data from this cell enabled us to show that AP2IX-1 is sufficient to drive a switching of surface antigen expression toward that resembling the sexual stages of the parasite.
evidence: Supported by experimental data

claim: AP2IX-1 contributes to remodeling of the surface antigen repertoire during differentiation.
source: Assuming this change in mRNA abundance translates into a change in protein levels of TGGT1_222305, which is predicted to contain a transmembrane domain, and SRS22C, which is strongly indicated to be a surface antigen like the rest of SRS, our data indicate that AP2IX-1 contributes to remodeling of the surface antigen repertoire during differentiation.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data

claim: AP2IX-1 may play a causal role in controlling the sexual differentiation of Toxoplasma.
source: Furthermore, this suggests AP2IX-1 may play a causal role in controlling the sexual differentiation of Toxoplasma.
evidence: Speculation based on experimental data

claim: The family of AP2 transcription factors was originally found to regulate stress response and floral sexual differentiation in plants.
source: Considering that the family of AP2 transcription factors was originally found to regulate stress response and floral sexual differentiation in plants, our finding suggests the biological role of AP2 family in Toxoplasma is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: Established knowledge about AP2 transcription factors

claim: The biological role of AP2 family in Toxoplasma is evolutionarily conserved.
source: Considering that the family of AP2 transcription factors was originally found to regulate stress response and floral sexual differentiation in plants, our finding suggests the biological role of AP2 family in Toxoplasma is evolutionarily conserved.
evidence: Inference based on experimental findings and evolutionary knowledge

claim: Cross-species clusters that share significant similarity in the expression of orthologous genes were identified between Plasmodium and Toxoplasma.
source: While Plasmodium and Toxoplasma undergo distinct modes of cell replication and asexual development, we identified cross-species clusters that share significant similarity in the expression of orthologous genes.
evidence: Direct statement of finding

claim: The timing of expression in gene sets involved in cell cycle are conserved in the erythrocytic cycle of Plasmodium berghei.
source: We discovered that the timing of expression in gene sets involved in cell cycle are conserved in the erythrocytic cycle of Plasmodium berghei.
evidence: Direct statement of finding
